figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Reasoning at constant memory. (a) EdgeRock-4B leads the displayed 7B–14B bounded-state models on six text metrics; AIME averages 2024–2026 equally. (b) Configuration-derived BF16 attention KV capacity per sequence (log axes). EdgeRock uses 72 MiB, 99.1% less than Qwen3.5-4B at 256K. (c) Top: output-token throughput for 32K input and 32K output with repeated prompts, including prefill time, at each model’s best measured batch (Appendix Table 19); EdgeRock achieves 6.42$\times$ Qwen3.5-4B’s throughput. Bottom: cumulative decode rate for 128K input and 128K output at batch size 1. All runs use BF16 weights and KV on one Hopper 80GB GPU.
figures.headline: EdgeRock-4B leads displayed 7B–14B bounded-state models and needs 99.1% less attention cache than Qwen3.5-4B at 256K.
citing_sentences: Its 72 MiB of attention KV is 99.1% smaller than Qwen3.5-4B’s at 256K (Figure 1b).

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: EdgeRock architecture. (a) Text and image features share a decoder combining recurrence, local attention, and RMA. (b) Per KV group, admission selects up to 1,024 records from the committed bank and 256 writer-generated candidates. Selections become readable in the next block. (c) Current queries read committed anchors; null attention and a query-conditioned signed gate control their contribution to the residual stream alongside local attention.
figures.headline: The architecture pairs recurrence and local attention with RMA, where admission keeps up to 1,024 records per KV group.

figures.caption: Bounded-state capability. (a) Equal-weight mean across 29 text benchmarks. (b) Equal-weight mean across AIME 2024–2026. Both panels order models by the 29-benchmark mean. EdgeRock-4B ranks first in both summaries among 17 models spanning 1.5B–14B. W2047 identifies Phi-3 Medium’s configured 2,047-token attention window.
figures.headline: EdgeRock-4B ranks first among 17 models spanning 1.5B–14B on both the 29-benchmark mean and the AIME mean.

On AIME 2024–2026, EdgeRock-4B reaches an 82.9% mean pass@1, compared with 18.8% for RWKV-7 G1j 13.3B, the strongest bounded-state AIME comparator (Figure 3).

figures.caption: Capability after conversion. Bars report EdgeRock-4B minus its Qwen3.5-4B source backbone in percentage points, ordered from largest to smallest. Blue highlights the eight benchmark gains; aligned columns give absolute scores (%).
figures.headline: After conversion, EdgeRock-4B exceeds its Qwen3.5-4B source on eight of 29 text benchmarks, including Massive Multitask Language Understanding and HumanEval.
citing_sentences: EdgeRock-4B exceeds Qwen3.5-4B on eight of 29 text benchmarks, including MMLU, MMLU-Pro, MMLU-Redux, SuperGPQA, HumanEval, and MBPP (Figure 4).

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Distant-memory reasoning. (a) Query accuracy and complete-context success after RMA adaptation (M0), joint adaptation (R), supervised fine-tuning (S), and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Complete-context success requires all four answers to be correct. (b) The final model with all eight RMA modules on or off; recurrence and local attention remain active in both settings. With RMA enabled, EdgeRock correctly answers 94.1% of queries and completes 80.1% of contexts across retrieval, state updates, cross-document combination, and variable binding.
figures.headline: Query accuracy reaches 94.1% in the final model, and disabling all RMA modules drops it to 0.4%.
citing_sentences: Section 7 tracks memory accuracy after each stage (Figure 5a).

On 256 contexts of 16K to 130,000 input tokens, with four queries each covering retrieval, state updates, cross-document combination, and variable binding, it answers 94.1% of queries; with RMA disabled, it answers 0.4% (Figure 5).

Memory is learned early and kept through post-training: query accuracy rises from 79.4% after RMA adaptation (M0) to 96.1% after joint adaptation (R) and stays at 94.1% in the final model (Figure 5a).

abstract: We present EdgeRock, a family of multimodal models that deliver strong reasoning at constant memory. Most models keep reasoning history in a key–value (KV) cache that grows with every token, consuming accelerator memory, limiting concurrent requests, and competing with perception and control on edge devices. With fixed history, memory is allocated once and never runs out, however long the model reasons. Constant memory alone is not new: bounded-state models (recurrent, state-space, and sliding-window) already achieve it, but often at the cost of reasoning, because they cannot keep the distant details that later reasoning needs. We therefore introduce Rock Memory Anchors (RMA): the model learns what is worth remembering and stores it as KV records in a fixed-size bank, directly readable however far back the source lies. EdgeRock-4B, our first open-source release, supports text and image reasoning and reaches 82.9% mean pass@1 on AIME 2024–2026, while the bounded-state models we evaluate reach at most 18.8%, even at 14B scale. This result is on par with leading compact models whose memory grows with reasoning. Compared with its source model, EdgeRock-4B uses up to 99.1% less KV cache and delivers up to 6.42$\times$ higher end-to-end batch throughput.

sections.body: The section argues that a growing key–value cache raises accelerator memory costs and makes edge memory budgets unpredictable. Bounded-state models have fixed memory, but none of 16 evaluated models exceeds 18.8% on AIME 2024–2026. The authors introduce Rock Memory Anchors (RMA), in which a learned writer and scorer keep up to 1,024 records per KV group in a fixed bank. Local attention covers the most recent 1,024 tokens. Local attention and RMA together hold attention KV at 72 MiB per sequence at any length. Table 1 lists the claims and their supporting results.
sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.headline: Growing reasoning caches strain serving and edge budgets, and bounded-state models lose reasoning, so EdgeRock adds learned fixed-size anchors.

sections.body: EdgeRock-4B adapts the Qwen3.5-4B language backbone. It keeps 24 Gated DeltaNet layers and replaces the eight full-attention layers with a 1,024-position sliding window plus an independent RMA module in each of eight blocks. The writer, admission, query, key, and value projections of RMA are separate from the backbone. The model is converted in four stages: RMA adaptation (M0), joint adaptation (R), supervised post-training (S), and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. Table 2 lists 372M RMA parameters and a residual width of 2,560.
sections.heading: 2 How is EdgeRock built?
sections.headline: EdgeRock-4B converts Qwen3.5-4B by replacing full attention with a 1,024-position window plus an RMA module in four training stages.

sections.body: A learned writer produces a candidate record for each token, and a causal scorer gives each KV group a retention priority. Every 256 tokens, the committed bank and new candidates compete, and each group keeps its highest-scoring 1,024 records. Selected candidates become readable in the next block, while local attention covers recent tokens. A query reads the bank with a null item, so an empty bank returns zero. A signed gate between -2 and 2 scales each head's output. Records discarded by admission cannot re-enter the global top K, so the bank keeps the highest-priority records from all completed blocks.
sections.heading: 3 How does RMA preserve distant information?
sections.headline: RMA keeps the highest-scoring records in a fixed bank of 1,024 per group, updated every 256 tokens, and any query can read them.

sections.body: Recurrent state, the local window, and anchor banks have bounded capacity, so the history allocation is O(1) in prompt plus generated length. Table 3 totals 97.76 MiB per sequence, of which 71.97 MiB is attention KV. For the same eight attention layers, a 256K-token full-attention cache needs 8 GiB, which the paper states is a 99.1% reduction in attention KV. Decoding time is stated as O(N) for N generated tokens, while full attention needs O(PN+N^2) attention work during decode.
sections.heading: 4 What stays constant as context grows?
sections.headline: Persistent history per sequence stays fixed in size however long the model reasons, unlike a full-attention cache that grows with each token.

sections.body: Five comparisons each isolate one question: 16 bounded-state models, the source model Qwen3.5-4B to measure what conversion costs, compact growing-history models, RMA enabled versus disabled, and four compact models for decode rate, batch throughput, and GPU memory. The overall mean weights all 29 primary metrics equally, and AIME averages the 2024–2026 editions equally. Memory and visual evaluations use reference arithmetic, while runtime experiments use the optimized profiles in Section 8.
sections.heading: 5 Evaluation design
sections.headline: The evaluation compares 28 models on 29 text benchmarks and measures visual reasoning, distant memory, and long-sequence inference.

sections.body: Among 17 bounded-state models, EdgeRock-4B ranks first on 24 of 29 text benchmarks, and its 29-benchmark mean exceeds AHN-GDN Qwen2.5 14B by 23.8 percentage points. Against its source, it retains 96.3% of the AIME mean and reaches 97.5% on MATH-500. Against compact growing-history models, its AIME score of 82.9% lies between Granite4.2-3B at 82.2% and Qwen3.5-4B at 86.1%. On six visual benchmarks it reaches 84.9% against 89.1% for Qwen3.5-4B. The bounded-state baselines differ in training data and post-training, so the comparison shows where the class stands.
sections.heading: 6 Does strong reasoning survive constant memory?
sections.headline: EdgeRock-4B reaches 82.9% on AIME 2024–2026 and retains 96.3% of its Qwen3.5-4B source's AIME mean.

sections.body: On 256 contexts of 16K to 130,000 input tokens, with four queries each, the final model answers 94.1% of 1,024 queries. When all eight RMA modules are disabled at inference, correct answers fall from 964 to 4 of 1,024, while recurrence and local attention remain active. Query accuracy is 79.4% after RMA adaptation, 96.1% after joint adaptation, and 94.1% in the final model. Complete-context success is 80.1% overall but only 53.1% on variable binding. Paired changes to distant evidence give correct answers on 89.8% of pairs whose answer should change and 96.5% of pairs whose answer should stay the same.
sections.heading: 7 Do distant answers depend on RMA?
sections.headline: Disabling RMA at inference drops query accuracy from 94.1% to 0.4%, showing distant answers flow through the anchor bank.

sections.body: Measured on one Hopper 80GB GPU with BF16 weights and KV, EdgeRock-4B decodes a single request at 233.7 tokens/s through 128K output, 1.54× Qwen3.5-4B's rate. With 254K input and 2K output, it decodes at 226.6 tokens/s versus 133.9 for Qwen3.5-4B. Long-generation throughput averages 4.94× Qwen3.5-4B and 7.18× LFM2.5-2.6B across 4K to 32K inputs. Full-attention Qwen3.5-4B fills its cache after a few dozen concurrent sequences at 32K input and 32K output. Weighted decoding reaches 12,497 tokens/s at batch size 512, or 24.4 tokens/s per active sequence. The authors attribute these gains to fixed history.
sections.heading: 8 What does constant memory buy in deployment?
sections.headline: EdgeRock-4B runs 512 long-generation sequences at once on one accelerator and averages 4.94 times Qwen3.5-4B's end-to-end throughput.

sections.body: The conclusion states that fixed history makes memory a property of the model rather than of the input. The authors name three deployments: a robot running perception and reasoning in one loop, a dedicated chip holding its full history on-chip, and an agent whose memory does not grow with each tool call. They list future work: scaling RMA to larger backbones, applying the conversion to other hybrid architectures, and extending anchors to images, audio, and sensor streams. Each anchor records its source position, so what a model chose to remember can be inspected directly.
sections.heading: 9 Conclusion
sections.headline: Fixed history makes memory a design-time property, which the authors argue lets robots, chips, and agents plan capacity before reasoning.

sections.body: Appendix A gives sampling, scoring, and verifier rules for text, visual, and memory evaluations. Appendix B reports the bounded-state comparators on 29 benchmarks across mathematics, knowledge, and reasoning tables, and Appendix C reports the growing-history models. Tables 19 to 21 hold throughput and GPU memory measurements. Appendix E specifies the state a continuing request owns, the forward procedure, and the rules for continuation and chunking.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists the text and visual evaluation protocols, bounded-state and compact benchmark tables, runtime tables, and the state-ownership specification.
